newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - FTSE spreads used to hedge market moves.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FTSE spreads used to hedge market moves.

text.p: A complex deal in the UK's FTSE 100 index was struck on Tuesday involving the purchase of a put spread and the sale of a call spread against buying FTSE futures, dealers said.
"It was a cheap way of allowing the trader to make money if the market goes up and limit losses if it comes down," said one dealer.
The call spread consisted of buying 1,000 December 4600 calls at 106p and selling 1,000 December 4500 calls at 146p.
The put spread involved selling 1,000 December 3800 puts at 67p and buying 1,000 December 4000 puts at 108p.
The call spread had a net credit of 46p and the put spread had a net debit of 40p making an overall credit of 1p.
In general, if the FTSE rises but does not go above 4500, the calls will be worthless and profits will come from the long futures position.
These profits will be eroded by the call spread as the index goes above 4500. There is also a risk of being assigned the December 4500 short calls.
Similarly if the market does not fall below 4000 the puts will be worthless and the trader will lose 40p from the put spread.
A further fall by the index to below 3800 will entitle the trader to receive credit arising from the difference between the put option strike prices.
By 1555 GMT, spot FTSE was up 9.4 at 4267.2, while March futures were up six points 4265.
In stock options one large trade was the purchase of 1,000 July 160 puts at 22-1/2p in British Steel. And in GEC, 1,000 May 390 calls were bought at 20p.
British Steel shares slipped 1-3/4p to 146-1/2p and GEC added 3-1/2p to 391-1/2p.
